title: Dried salmon
translation: Shijō Takachika once had dried salmon served at the emperor's table. Someone said, "You can't serve His Majesty something as common as that." Takachika heard about it and said: "If His Majesty didn't eat salmon, fair enough. But what's wrong with salmon dried plain? He eats plain dried sweetfish, doesn't he?"
original: {四条大納言|しでうのだいなごん}{隆親卿|たかちかのきやう}、{乾鮭|からざけ}といふものを{供御|ぐご}に{参|まゐ}らせられたりけるを、「かく{怪|あや}しきもの{参|まゐ}るやうあらじ。」と{人|ひと}の{申|まう}しけるを{聞|き}きて、
{大納言|だいなごん}、「{鮭|さけ}といふ{魚|うを}まゐらぬことにてあらむにこそあれ。
{鮭|さけ}の{素干|しらぼし}なでふことかあらむ。
{鮎|あゆ}の{素干|しらぼし}はまゐらぬかは。」と{申|まう}されけり。
literal: Lord Takachika, the Shijō Major Counsellor, had a thing called dried salmon served for the emperor's meal; hearing someone say, 'There can be no way that such a lowly thing is eaten (by the emperor)',
the Major Counsellor said, 'If salmon were a fish that is not eaten (by him), then it would be so.
What could be wrong with salmon dried plain?
Is sweetfish dried plain not eaten (by him)?'

notes.text: Fujiwara no Takachika of the Shijō house, a major counsellor in the thirteenth century. The 1925 edition notes that he was the son of Takahira.
{乾鮭|からざけ}: salmon gutted and dried whole. Salmon came from the north and east, and dried salmon counted as plain, everyday food.

Two meanings of the same verb in one story. {参|まゐ}らす: 'to serve, to offer' (humble, towards the emperor). {参|まゐ}る without す: 'to eat' (respectful, of the emperor). The objection and Takachika's answer both turn on whether His Majesty 'eats' it.

notes.quote: まゐらぬことにてあらむにこそあれ
notes.text: む … にこそあれ: 'if it were…, then (you would have a point)'. He grants the objection only for a case that does not exist.
{素干|しらぼし}: dried without salt. Sweetfish ({鮎|あゆ}), a small river fish, was a delicacy, and served dried the same way.
なでふ: 'what kind of', from なにといふ. かは in the next line: another rhetorical question. Two in a row, and the argument is over.
